clue.text: Boss with home near centre of Beverley

parts.note: gaff is British slang for a person's home

indicators.note: the centre of a word is its middle letters, here the two in the middle of Beverley

explanation.surface: A manager lives close to the middle of the Yorkshire town of Beverley.
explanation.walkthrough: 'centre of' takes the middle two letters of the eight-letter Beverley, ER. GAFF is everyday British slang for one's house.
explanation.definitionFit: Gaffer is informal British for a foreman or manager, someone in charge.

clue.text: A sack in flames

parts.note: to sack someone is to fire them from a job

explanation.surface: A bag of goods catches fire.
explanation.definitionFit: Something afire is burning, ablaze.

clue.text: Female has cause to enrol English male as society member

indicators.note: to enrol something is to take it in as a member, so the cause word takes in the other letters

parts.note: a reason is a cause or ground for something

explanation.surface: A woman has grounds to sign up an Englishman as a member of some club.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to enrol' is the container signal: the English male is taken into the cause as a club takes in a new member, which suits the Masonic surface.
explanation.definitionFit: A Freemason belongs to the fraternal society of Freemasonry.

clue.text: Male debtor, perhaps, put on bail

annotationWithheld.why: Male debtor, perhaps, put on bail (6): REMAND is MAN inside RED, but 'debtor, perhaps' must both give RED (in the red) and signal the containment (a man IN the red), one phrase doing two jobs
annotationWithheld.clue: Male debtor, perhaps, put on bail

clue.text: Transport silver in the city

parts.note: a car is a means of transport

indicators.note: in places the silver symbol inside the word the

parts.note: Ag is the chemical symbol for silver

explanation.surface: Moving silver about in town.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in the city' reads as a single phrase, but 'the' is fodder and 'in' is the container signal; only 'city' defines.
explanation.definitionFit: Carthage was the ancient Phoenician city in North Africa destroyed by Rome.

clue.text: Visions of rooks flying?

parts.note: in chess the rook is also called a castle
something flying is up in the air

explanation.surface: Daydreams of black birds wheeling about.
explanation.walkthrough: Rooks look like the birds, but they are chess pieces, also called castles.
explanation.definitionFit: Castles in the air are daydreams or impractical schemes, visions that will never be real.

clue.text: Comfy chair in play area on cruise ship

parts.note: a rec is short for recreation ground, a British public play area
a liner is a large passenger ship used for cruises

explanation.surface: An armchair placed in the games room aboard an ocean liner.
explanation.walkthrough: A REC is a recreation ground, a British park or playing field.
explanation.definitionFit: A recliner is an upholstered armchair whose back tips back for lounging.

clue.text: Smell unpleasant American decomposed matter

parts.note: to hum is British slang for giving off a bad smell
US is short for American, as in the US

explanation.surface: Rotting stuff from the States gives off a nasty whiff.
explanation.definitionFit: Humus is the dark organic part of soil formed by rotting plant and animal remains.

clue.text: Be socially active — buy everyone a drink

explanation.surface: Party life described as standing everyone drinks.
explanation.definitionFit: To get around is to go out and mix widely; to get a round is to buy drinks for the whole group.

clue.text: Background notes?

parts.note: notes sound like jottings, but they are musical notes played softly in the background of shops and lifts

explanation.definitionFit: Piped music is recorded music played over speakers in public places as a backdrop.

clue.text: Friend regularly embattled

indicators.note: regularly takes every other letter, here the second, fourth, sixth and eighth of embattled

explanation.surface: A pal who is constantly under siege.
explanation.definitionFit: Mate is informal British for a pal or companion.

clue.text: Much of large mine collapsed … in this novel

indicators.note: something collapsed has fallen apart, so the letters are rearranged
much of a word is most of it, so the last letter of large is dropped

explanation.surface: Most of a large mine caves in, as described in a novel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Much of' trims large to LARG, and 'collapsed' rearranges LARG with MINE.
explanation.definitionFit: Germinal is Zola's 1885 novel about a coal miners' strike, so a mine collapse fits it.

clue.text: Arrange cover for home, certainly

parts.note: to be in is to be at home
sure is used to mean certainly, as in 'sure, come along'

explanation.surface: Taking out a household policy, definitely.
explanation.definitionFit: To insure something is to take out a policy that covers it against loss.

clue.text: Hardy heroine set about nursing small son

indicators.note: nursing means holding in the arms, so one piece holds another inside it
about here means turned round, so the word set is read backwards

parts.note: taken as written
S is the abbreviation for both small and son

explanation.surface: A tough heroine settles down nursing her little boy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' turns SET into TES, and 'nursing' puts S inside it, between E and S. 'Hardy' looks like toughness, but it is Thomas Hardy.
explanation.definitionFit: Tess Durbeyfield is the title heroine of Thomas Hardy's Tess of the d'Urbervilles.

clue.text: Tricky clue can take time — I'll come in to explain

indicators.note: to come in is to enter, so this letter goes inside the rest
a tricky clue is one twisted out of shape, so its letters are rearranged

parts.note: a date is a point in time
I'll is I will, so the I is what comes in

explanation.surface: A hard clue can take ages, so the setter says they will step in to clarify.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tricky' is the anagram signal on 'clue' alone, giving ELUC; 'come in' then drops I into the gap between that and the time word. 'can' and 'take' are linking words.
explanation.definitionFit: To elucidate is to make clear, to throw light on something.

clue.text: Make it very clear — rubbish pollutes

indicators.note: rubbish as a verb-like signal says the letters are trashed and rearranged

explanation.surface: Stating plainly that litter fouls the environment.
explanation.definitionFit: To spell something out is to explain it in plain detail.

clue.text: Looking to get about without tasting alcohol is character-forming

annotationWithheld.why: Looking to get about without tasting alcohol is character-forming (9): LEERING (looking) about TT, where the whole phrase 'without tasting alcohol' means TT (teetotal); the checker reads that leaf as a deletion folded into 'tasting' (TT runs through it) and allows no wrongRole, and the phrase cannot be split without misparsing
annotationWithheld.clue: Looking to get about without tasting alcohol is character-forming

clue.text: Liberals entering advertisement for political researcher

indicators.note: entering means going into, so one piece goes inside the other

parts.note: a poster is a printed advertisement on a wall
L is the abbreviation for Liberal, doubled for the plural

explanation.surface: Liberal Party members join an advert campaign aimed at a political analyst.
explanation.walkthrough: 'entering' is the container signal. Liberals are two Ls because each L stands for one Liberal.
explanation.definitionFit: A pollster runs opinion polls, researching voters' views.

clue.text: Don't take bend on road from summit

parts.note: a turn is a bend in a road
on the road from a summit one is going down

explanation.surface: A warning about a hairpin bend on the road coming off a mountain.
explanation.definitionFit: To turn down an offer is to refuse it, not accept it.

clue.text: In addition, daughter's admitted creating trouble

indicators.note: admitted means let in, so one piece is let inside the other

parts.note: too means in addition, also
D is the abbreviation for daughter

explanation.surface: Also, the daughter has confessed to making a fuss.
explanation.walkthrough: 'admitted' is the container signal: the daughter is let in among the letters for 'in addition'.
explanation.definitionFit: A to-do is a commotion or fuss.

clue.text: Transported, when given a kiss

explanation.surface: Someone carried somewhere and kissed on arrival.
explanation.definitionFit: Bussed means carried by bus; buss is also an old word for a kiss.

clue.text: Note girl rejected (or girl rejected note) in prayer book

parts.note: mi is the third note of the sol-fa scale

indicators.note: rejected means thrown back, so the girl word is read backwards

parts.note: a lass is a girl

explanation.surface: A choirgirl turned down a part in the prayer book.
explanation.walkthrough: The bracketed half says the same backwards: LASS then MI (IM), the whole run 'rejected', gives the same word, because the answer reverses its own pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: A missal is the book of prayers and texts used for saying Mass.

clue.text: Consume some delicious coffee

indicators.note: some says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: Drink a bit of tasty coffee.
explanation.definitionFit: To scoff is British slang for eating greedily, wolfing food down.

clue.text: Medic calls round after 45 minutes?

indicators.note: after puts the reversed piece after the first in the answer

parts.note: 45 minutes is three quarters of an hour, so three quarters of the word hour

indicators.note: round means turned round, so the calls word is read backwards

parts.note: to call someone something is to name them

explanation.surface: A doctor makes house calls after being kept waiting three quarters of an hour.
explanation.walkthrough: 'round' is the reversal signal and 'after' orders the pieces. '45 minutes' is three quarters of an hour, so three of the four letters of HOUR. A houseman is a British junior hospital doctor.
explanation.definitionFit: Houseman is the British term for a junior doctor in a hospital's first post.

clue.text: Sign of tooth decay, with top coming off

indicators.note: in a down clue the top is the first letter, which is removed

parts.note: caries is the medical term for tooth decay

explanation.surface: Evidence of a rotting tooth whose crown has broken off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'with top coming off' drops the first letter C of CARIES.
explanation.definitionFit: Aries the ram is the first sign of the zodiac.

clue.text: I try holding a villain

indicators.note: holding means clasping inside, so one piece goes within the other

parts.note: a go is a try or attempt

explanation.surface: Someone makes an attempt while carrying a bad guy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'holding' puts A between I and GO.
explanation.definitionFit: Iago is the scheming villain of Shakespeare's Othello.

clue.text: Is part-time training sufficient to get such comradeship?

indicators.note: training shapes and reworks something, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Asking whether occasional practice is enough to build a bond among players.
explanation.walkthrough: 'training' rearranges the ten letters of IS and PART-TIME.
explanation.definitionFit: Team spirit is the fellowship and loyalty felt among members of a group.

clue.text: Sailor's experience, going round distant Republic's capital

indicators.note: going round means encircling, so the first word surrounds the next

parts.note: to see something is to experience it
afar means far away, distant

indicators.note: a capital is a first letter, here of Republic

explanation.surface: A sailor travels far and visits a republic's capital city.
explanation.walkthrough: 'going round' is the container signal on the experience word, and 'capital' takes the first letter of Republic. The 's of 'Sailor's' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A seafarer is someone who travels by sea, a mariner.

clue.text: Girl talked of joke compilation

parts.note: Di is a girl's name, short for Diana

indicators.note: talked of says the next word is to be heard spoken, not read

parts.note: a jest is a joke

explanation.surface: A woman spoke about an anthology of jokes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'talked of' turns JEST into its sound-twin GEST.
explanation.definitionFit: A digest is a compilation or summary of collected material.
